Threat.value: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
Being superalert or watchful or on guard
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think

Memory.value: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: I have permanently changed for the worse
You can never know who will harm you
I am permanently an outsider now

issues.item: Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control
issues.explanation: Restricting eating to feel in control is not well supported by the rest of the profile. The other endorsed items center on partner-violence-related threat monitoring, hypervigilance, sensory memory, and danger appraisals. In contrast, restrictive eating reflects a different coping theme that is not echoed elsewhere in Threat, Memory, or Negative Appraisals, and it sits awkwardly with the formulation in which Maladaptive Strategies feed Threat. Scanning surroundings and mirror checking plausibly amplify threat, but strict eating control does not connect clearly to the described trauma pattern.

vignette: The night everything fractured, Linh Nguyen was twenty-eight when her partner's temper finally broke. It began over a spilled glass, but within minutes the living room air turned thick with his breathing. She remembered the sickening crack of his fist against the drywall, the way his eyes rolled back into a white, unrecognizable glare, and then the heavy ceramic lamp toppling toward her. She dove under the coffee table, the wood splintering as it struck where her head had been a second before. When she crawled out, the room was wrecked, but what stayed with her most was the glint of a shattered picture frame on the floor, its glass jagged and catching the hallway light just like the broken bottle he had thrown moments before. That night, her body had locked itself into a state of frozen alarm before her mind could even process the danger, a physiological surrender to panic that would never truly leave her. In the weeks that followed, the past did not settle; it pooled inside her. The event arrived not as a coherent story but as fragmented pieces that refused to fit together-the smell of his cologne, the metallic ring of a thrown shoe, the sudden silence after a slammed door. Whenever she closed her eyes, those disconnected fragments would snap into a photographic recall, just like looking at photographs of it in her mind, complete with the terror on recall that made her breath catch. This relentless flooding of the past directly fed her growing sense of isolation; remembering the event with such visceral clarity convinced her that she had permanently changed for the worse. The memories themselves compelled her to adopt rigid safety rituals, leading her to constantly scan her home office for signs of threat. As a tutor, she had once found solace in guiding students through literature, but now the quiet of her study felt like a trap. The negative appraisals she carried acted as a crucible for her self-view. She was certain that you could never know who would harm you again, and that lingering dread slowly seeped into her recollections, tinting every remembered detail with fresh suspicion. Carrying these negative appraisals directly poisoned the way the past resurfaced; because she believed she was permanently an outsider now, the memories stopped feeling like historical records and started feeling like ongoing warnings. The terror on recall intensified, each fragmented piece snapping into place with a violent clarity that left her trembling. As months bled into a year, the habits she adopted to stay safe began to dictate her own nervous system. Every time she forced herself to look in the mirror, her pulse spiked; every time she scanned the environment for potential weapons or dangerous objects, her shoulders locked tight. These maladaptive strategies directly fed her threat system, amplifying her hypervigilance towards people until a simple knock at the door sent her retreating. The sheer exhaustion of maintaining this alert posture then bled back into her memory processing, as the threat monitoring itself triggered the very intrusions she was trying to outrun. Her husband noticed how she jumped at household noises and systematically moved sharp objects to drawers. She tried to explain that she felt fundamentally different, but the words stuck in her throat. It was the isolation that finally pushed her to the clinic. After a vivid episode where a dropped pen sent her into a full physiological panic, she realized she could no longer sustain the vigilance alone. She sat in the intake office today, acutely aware of the heavy paperweights on the reception desk and the polished floor that reflected the doorway behind the therapist. What frightened her most was that the safety she craved felt impossible to build, but what she was hoping for was simply to quiet the noise in her head. She wanted to learn how to sit in a room without counting exits, to trust that a glance in the mirror would not summon the past, and to finally believe she was more than the damage she had survived.
